item.title: Elder Uttarapāla: I am truly virtuous, Reflecting on good purpose. I have abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, Which are the world’s confusion. Born…
item.description:
Elder Uttarapāla:

I am truly virtuous,
Reflecting on good purpose.
I have abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,
Which are the world’s confusion.

Born in Māra’s realm,
Struck by strong darts,
Yet I have escaped
Māra’s snare.

All sensual desires are destroyed,
All forms of existence are demolished.
The path of birth and death is ended —
Now there is no further becoming.

From: Theragāthā 3.12
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating the Four Noble Truths that you and I have wandered and wandered through this long course.…
item.description:
“Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating the Four Noble Truths that you and I have wandered and wandered through this long course. What four? Because of not realizing, not penetrating the noble truth of suffering, monks, you and I have wandered and wandered through this long course … the noble truth of the origin of suffering … the noble truth of the cessation of suffering … Because of not realizing, not penetrating the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, monks, you and I have wandered and wandered through this long course. But now, monks, the noble truth of suffering has been realized and penetrated. The noble truth of the origin of suffering has been realized and penetrated. The noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized and penetrated. The noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been realized and penetrated. Cut off is craving for existence; destroyed is what leads to renewed existence. Now there is no further becoming.” The Blessed One said this … the Teacher further said:

From not seeing the four noble truths
As they really are,
One wanders for a long time
Through many births.
But when these are seen,
The root of rebirth is pulled out,
The root of suffering is cut off —
Now there is no further becoming.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.21
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - “What do you think, Mālukyaputta? Regarding forms cognizable by the eye that you have not seen, never saw before, do not see now, and…
item.description:
- “What do you think, Mālukyaputta? Regarding forms cognizable by the eye that you have not seen, never saw before, do not see now, and do not wish to see — do you have any desire, lust, or craving for them?” - “No, venerable sir.” - “Regarding sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … touches cognizable by the body that you have not felt, never felt before, do not feel now, and do not wish to feel — do you have any desire, lust, or craving for them?” - “No, venerable sir.”

Seeing a form, if one’s mind is infatuated,
Attending to a pleasing sign,
The mind is attached to the feeling,
Clinging to the form remains.
His feelings increase,
Manyfold, born from form —
Greed and hurtful thoughts
Harm his mind.
Thus accumulating suffering,
He is said to be far from Nibbāna.

Hearing a sound, mind infatuated …
Smelling an odor …
Tasting a flavor …
If one’s mind is infatuated,
Attending to a pleasing sign,
The mind attached to the feeling,
Clinging to the flavor remains.
His feelings increase,
Manyfold, born from flavor —
Greed and hurtful thoughts
Harm his mind.
Thus accumulating suffering,
He is said to be far from Nibbāna.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.95
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When…
item.description:
“Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, consciousness becomes established. When consciousness is established and grows, there is a leaning (nati). When there is a leaning, there is a going to a state of rebirth. When there is a going to a state of rebirth, there is future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the origination of this whole mass of suffering. Monks, if one does not intend, does not plan, and has no tendency towards anything, there is no basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is no basis, consciousness does not become established. When consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no leaning. When there is no leaning, there is no going to a state of rebirth. When there is no going to a state of rebirth, there is no future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.40

item.title: “Monks, there are these five defilements of the mind because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five defilements of the mind because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. What five? Sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt. These five defilements of the mind, monks, because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.23
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Sensual desires are many, sweet, and agreeable, Disquieting the mind in many ways. Seeing the danger in these strands of pleasure, I went forth, great…
item.description:
Sensual desires are many, sweet, and agreeable,
Disquieting the mind in many ways.
Seeing the danger in these strands of pleasure,
I went forth, great king!
Like fruits falling from a tree,
Both young and old, when the body breaks,
Seeing this, I went forth,
The ascetic life is supreme,
Great king!

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “Monks, suppose a man is struck by an arrow, and then they strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the feeling…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose a man is struck by an arrow, and then they strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the feeling of both arrows. So too, monks, an untaught ordinary person, when touched by a painful feeling, sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. He experiences two feelings — a bodily feeling and a mental feeling. Touched by that painful feeling, he feels aversion. Because he feels aversion toward that painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling persists. Touched by that painful feeling, he delights in sensual pleasures. Why? Because, monks, the untaught ordinary person knows no escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure. Delighting in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling persists. He does not know as it actually is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding these feelings. Not knowing as it actually is the origination … and escape regarding these feelings, the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling persists. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. This, monks, is called an untaught ordinary person who is bound by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is bound by suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.6
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Here, brahmin, a person is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not…
item.description:
“Here, brahmin, a person is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, not free from craving. Then a severe illness arises for him. Affected by that severe illness, he thinks: ‘Truly, agreeable sensual pleasures will leave me,’ or ‘I will leave agreeable sensual pleasures.’ He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. This, brahmin, is a person who is subject to death, fearful, and falls into terror at the thought of death.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.184
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, suppose a person is being swept away by a river that is lovely and pleasant. A man with good eyesight, standing on the bank,…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose a person is being swept away by a river that is lovely and pleasant. A man with good eyesight, standing on the bank, seeing him, says: ‘Good man, though you are being swept away by this lovely, pleasant river, further down there is a lake with waves and whirlpools, with crocodiles and demons. If you reach that place, you will die or suffer deadly pain.’ Then that person, hearing his words, struggles upstream with his hands and feet. Monks, I have given this simile to make the meaning clear. The meaning here is this: ‘The river,’ monks, is a synonym for craving. ‘Lovely and pleasant’ is a synonym for the six internal sense bases. ‘The lake further down’ is a synonym for the five lower fetters. ‘Waves’ is a synonym for anger and distress. ‘Whirlpools’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Crocodiles and demons’ is a synonym for women. ‘Struggling upstream’ is a synonym for renunciation. ‘Struggling with hands and feet’ is a synonym for arousing energy. ‘The man with good eyesight standing on the bank’ is a synonym for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”

From: Itivuttaka 109

item.title: O monks, these six sense bases — Where they are unrestrained, There suffering comes to be. Those who learn to guard them, To restrain and…
item.description:
O monks, these six sense bases —
Where they are unrestrained,
There suffering comes to be.
Those who learn to guard them,
To restrain and protect them,
With faith as their companion,
Dwell freed from sensual lust.

Seeing forms that are pleasing,
Seeing forms that are displeasing,
Restrain the path of lust
For forms that are pleasing —
Do not let the mind be defiled,
Thinking: ‘I do not delight in forms.’

Having heard sounds —
Pleasing and displeasing,
Do not be infatuated with pleasing sounds.
Restrain the mind’s aversion
For sounds that are displeasing,
Do not let the mind be defiled,
Thinking: ‘I do not delight in sounds.’

Having smelled fragrant, delightful odors,
Having smelled foul, loathsome odors —
Restrain aversion for loathsome odors,
And for delightful ones,
Do not let desire dominate.

Having tasted sweet flavors,
And also flavors that are not sweet,
Do not develop greed
When enjoying a sweet taste,
Do not utter words of opposition
When tasting what is not sweet.

When touched by pleasant contact,
Do not be infatuated with lust;
When touched by painful contact,
Do not be violently shaken.
For both contacts — pleasant and painful —
Remain equanimous,
Without approval or opposition,
Whatever contact may arise.

Those who follow proliferated perceptions,
Who are lost in conceptual proliferation,
Who act upon false thoughts —
Abandon all household activities
Born of the mind,
Practice restraint in your actions,
Directing yourself to the path of seclusion.

Thus, with the mind well-developed
Regarding these six sense bases,
Whatever contact occurs,
The mind is not disturbed.
Having subdued both greed and hatred,
O monk, go to the far shore,
Beyond the bonds of birth and death.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.94
📖 Read this sutta
